items.q: Name the four benefits of quantizing a model to INT8.
items.a_short: 4× smaller weights, less memory bandwidth, faster integer math on dedicated units, and lower energy per operation.
items.a_full: Energy is often the real driver on a phone: an INT8 multiply-accumulate costs roughly an order of magnitude less energy than FP32, and a DRAM access costs far more than either. Reducing bytes moved frequently matters more than reducing FLOPs.

options: Size, bandwidth, integer throughput and energy per op

items.q: Write the affine quantization formula and define each term.
items.a_short: `q = clamp(round(x/s) + z, q_min, q_max)` and dequantize as `x ≈ s·(q − z)`. `s` is the scale (step size), `z` is the zero-point.
items.a_full: For asymmetric INT8 over [x_min, x_max]: `s = (x_max − x_min)/255` and `z = round(q_min − x_min/s)`. The zero-point guarantees that real 0.0 maps exactly to an integer — essential, because padding and ReLU outputs must stay exactly zero or errors accumulate.
items.a_code:
s = (x_max - x_min) / (q_max - q_min)
z = round(q_min - x_min / s)
q = clip(round(x / s) + z, q_min, q_max)
x_hat = s * (q - z)

options: q = clamp(round(x/s) + z); x ≈ s(q − z)

items.q: Symmetric vs asymmetric quantization — when is each right?
items.a_short: Symmetric forces zero-point = 0 and uses a range centred on zero. Asymmetric allows a non-zero offset to fit a skewed range tightly.
items.a_full: Weights are roughly zero-centred, so symmetric is standard and cheaper — no cross-terms in the matmul. Activations after ReLU are one-sided ([0, max]), so symmetric would waste half the range; asymmetric fits them far better. The usual production choice is symmetric per-channel weights with asymmetric per-tensor activations.

options: Symmetric for activations, asymmetric for weights
Symmetric (z=0) for weights; asymmetric for one-sided activations like post-ReLU

items.q: Per-tensor vs per-channel quantization.
items.a_short: Per-tensor uses one scale for the whole weight tensor; per-channel uses one per output channel. Per-channel is far more accurate when channel ranges differ widely.
items.a_full: Depthwise convolutions are the classic case — their per-channel weight ranges can differ by orders of magnitude, and per-tensor quantization of MobileNet collapses accuracy. Per-channel costs a small vector of scales and is supported by essentially every modern runtime for weights. Activations stay per-tensor because their ranges are only known at runtime.

options: Per-channel uses one scale per output channel and is much better for depthwise convs
They are equivalent for all layers

items.q: PTQ vs QAT — the trade-off.
items.a_short: PTQ quantizes a trained model using a small calibration set — minutes, no labels. QAT simulates quantization during training so the model adapts — hours to days, needs the training pipeline.
items.a_full: Rule of thumb: try PTQ first. If INT8 accuracy drop is under ~1%, ship it. QAT recovers most of the remaining gap and is usually necessary for INT4, for depthwise-heavy architectures, and for small models with little redundancy.

options: QAT is faster to run than PTQ
PTQ is post-hoc with calibration data; QAT simulates quantization during training for better accuracy

items.q: What is a calibration dataset and what makes a good one?
items.a_short: A small unlabelled sample (typically 100-1000 inputs) run through the model to record activation ranges. It must be representative of production data.
items.a_full: Range-setting methods: min/max (simple, outlier-sensitive), percentile (clip the tail), MSE-optimal, and KL-divergence (TensorRT's approach, matching the quantized distribution to the float one). Calibrating on the wrong distribution is a leading cause of 'works in the lab, fails in the field'.

options: A labelled test set for accuracy measurement
A small unlabelled representative sample used to record activation ranges

items.q: How does gradient descent work through a rounding operation in QAT?
items.a_short: The Straight-Through Estimator: the forward pass rounds, the backward pass pretends the rounding was the identity function.
items.a_full: `round()` has zero gradient almost everywhere, which would kill learning. STE passes the incoming gradient through unchanged (usually clipped to the quantization range). It's a biased estimator but works well in practice. LSQ extends this by learning the scale parameter itself through the same trick.

options: Straight-Through Estimator: forward rounds, backward treats it as identity

items.q: Which parts of a network are most sensitive to quantization?
items.a_short: The first and last layers, depthwise convolutions, attention softmax and LayerNorm, and anything with a wide dynamic range or few channels.
items.a_full: Standard practice is to keep the first conv and the final classifier in higher precision — they're a tiny fraction of total FLOPs but carry outsized accuracy impact. Mixed-precision assignment via per-layer sensitivity analysis (quantize one layer at a time, measure the drop) is the systematic way to decide.

options: First/last layers, depthwise convs, softmax and LayerNorm

items.q: Dynamic vs static quantization.
items.a_short: Dynamic quantizes weights ahead of time but computes activation scales at runtime per batch. Static pre-computes activation scales from calibration.
items.a_full: Dynamic needs no calibration data and handles varying ranges well, which suits NLP/RNN workloads — but the runtime range computation costs time and usually blocks full integer execution on an NPU. Static is what you want for a fixed-function accelerator.

options: Dynamic computes activation scales at runtime; static uses calibration-derived scales

items.q: Why do large transformers resist naive INT8 quantization?
items.a_short: Systematic activation outliers — a few channels carry values 10-100× larger than the rest, so a per-tensor scale wastes almost all its range on them.
items.a_full: Fixes: LLM.int8() keeps outlier channels in FP16 and the rest in INT8. SmoothQuant migrates the difficulty from activations into weights with a per-channel scaling that the weights absorb, since weights quantize more easily. AWQ and GPTQ take weight-only routes, which suit memory-bound token-by-token decoding.

options: Systematic activation outliers in a few channels destroy per-tensor scaling

items.q: Structured vs unstructured pruning — which actually speeds things up?
items.a_short: Structured (whole channels, filters, heads) gives real speedup on any hardware. Unstructured (individual weights) gives high sparsity but needs sparse kernels to pay off.
items.a_full: A 90% unstructured-sparse model usually runs no faster on a standard NPU — dense matmul hardware can't exploit scattered zeros. NVIDIA's 2:4 semi-structured sparsity is the compromise: hardware-supported, 2× throughput, modest accuracy cost. For edge, prefer structured pruning or a smaller architecture outright.

options: Structured gives real speedup; unstructured needs sparse kernel support

items.q: What is the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis?
items.a_short: A dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that, trained from the *original* initialization, matches the full model's accuracy.
items.a_full: The procedure is iterative magnitude pruning: train, prune the smallest weights, rewind the survivors to their initial values, retrain. The rewind is the crucial part — the same mask with fresh random init performs much worse. On large models the rewind is usually to an early training step rather than step zero.

options: Random pruning works as well as magnitude pruning
A sparse subnetwork trained from the original init matches the dense model
Pruning after training is always lossless

items.q: How does knowledge distillation work, and why do soft targets help?
items.a_short: A small student is trained to match a large teacher's softened output distribution. Soft targets carry 'dark knowledge' — the relative similarity between wrong classes.
items.a_full: Loss = α·CE(student, hard labels) + (1−α)·T²·KL(student_T ‖ teacher_T), where temperature T>1 softens both distributions. The T² factor restores gradient magnitude, which scales as 1/T². Knowing that a given image is 'mostly cat, somewhat tiger, never truck' is far richer supervision than a one-hot label.

options: The student copies the teacher's weights
The student matches the teacher's softened output distribution, learning inter-class similarity
It only works for classification with 2 classes

items.q: How do you fold BatchNorm into the preceding convolution?
items.a_short: At inference BN is a fixed affine transform per channel, so its scale and shift can be absorbed into the conv's weights and bias — removing the BN layer entirely.
items.a_full: `W' = W · γ/√(σ² + ε)` and `b' = (b − μ)·γ/√(σ² + ε) + β`. This is free: fewer kernel launches, fewer memory round-trips, and it's mandatory before INT8 quantization because an unfolded BN introduces a float op in the middle of an integer pipeline.
items.a_code:
scale = gamma / sqrt(var + eps)
W_fold = W * scale.reshape(-1, 1, 1, 1)
b_fold = (b - mean) * scale + beta

options: BN is a fixed per-channel affine map at inference, absorbable into conv weights and bias

items.q: Why is operator fusion such a large win on edge hardware?
items.a_short: It avoids writing intermediate tensors to DRAM and reading them back. Memory traffic, not arithmetic, is usually the bottleneck.
items.a_full: Conv→BN→ReLU as three kernels means three full passes over the feature map. Fused into one, the intermediate values never leave registers or on-chip SRAM. This is why a FLOP reduction often fails to translate into a latency reduction — you cut the maths but not the data movement.

options: It reduces the number of parameters
It avoids DRAM round-trips for intermediate tensors

items.q: What is arithmetic intensity and why does it decide your optimization strategy?
items.a_short: FLOPs per byte of memory traffic. Low intensity means memory-bound — reducing FLOPs won't help; you need to reduce data movement.
items.a_full: The roofline model: performance is min(peak compute, intensity × bandwidth). Depthwise convs, elementwise ops and single-token LLM decoding are all memory-bound. Dense matmul with large tiles is compute-bound. Profile first — optimizing FLOPs on a memory-bound layer is wasted effort, which is the usual explanation for 'I cut FLOPs 4× and latency barely moved'.

options: FLOPs per byte of memory traffic, deciding compute- vs memory-bound

items.q: Latency vs throughput — why can't you optimize both?
items.a_short: Latency is time for one inference; throughput is inferences per second. Batching raises throughput by amortizing overhead, but each individual request waits longer.
items.a_full: Edge inference is almost always batch-size-1 and latency-bound — a camera pipeline needs this frame now. Server inference batches aggressively. This is why server benchmarks mislead on device: the hardware looks underutilized at batch 1 because there's no work to hide memory latency behind.

options: Latency is per-inference time; throughput is rate — batching helps throughput, hurts latency
Throughput matters most at the edge

items.q: On a mobile SoC, what are the CPU, GPU, DSP and NPU each good for?
items.a_short: CPU: control flow and unsupported ops, lowest startup cost. GPU: parallel float work, graphics interop. DSP/NPU: highest efficiency for quantized fixed-function inference, but a limited operator set.
items.a_full: On Snapdragon, the Hexagon processor with its tensor accelerator handles INT8/INT4 inference at by far the best performance per watt. The practical constraint is operator coverage: an unsupported op forces a fallback that splits the graph and costs a round-trip between memory spaces, which can erase the accelerator's advantage entirely.

options: NPU is best for all workloads
CPU for control flow, GPU for parallel float, DSP/NPU for efficient quantized inference with limited op support

items.q: What are SNPE, QNN and AIMET in Qualcomm's AI stack?
items.a_short: SNPE is the Snapdragon Neural Processing Engine runtime; QNN (AI Engine Direct) is the lower-level backend API across CPU/GPU/HTP; AIMET is the open-source model optimization library for quantization and compression.
items.a_full: Typical flow: train in PyTorch → optimize and simulate quantization with AIMET → export to ONNX → convert to a DLC or QNN context binary → run on the Hexagon tensor accelerator. AIMET's cross-layer equalization and bias correction are the techniques that make PTQ viable on depthwise-heavy mobile architectures.

options: SNPE is a runtime, QNN is the lower-level backend API, AIMET is the model optimization library

items.q: What is Cross-Layer Equalization and what problem does it solve?
items.a_short: It rescales weights between consecutive layers so each layer's per-channel ranges become more uniform, making per-tensor quantization viable.
items.a_full: It exploits the positive scaling equivariance of ReLU: `ReLU(s·x)/s = ReLU(x)`, so you can divide one layer's channel by s and multiply the next layer's corresponding input channel by s without changing the function. MobileNetV2's depthwise layers have wildly uneven channel ranges; CLE plus bias correction recovers most of the INT8 accuracy without any retraining.

options: It rescales weights across layers using ReLU scale equivariance to equalize channel ranges

items.q: How do you measure quantization damage layer by layer?
items.a_short: SQNR (signal-to-quantization-noise ratio) or cosine similarity between the float and quantized activation tensors, computed per layer.
items.a_full: SQNR = 10·log₁₀(‖x‖² / ‖x − x̂‖²) in dB. Plotting it per layer immediately shows which layer collapsed, long before end-to-end accuracy tells you anything. Watch for error compounding — a mid-network layer with modest SQNR can still wreck the output if later layers amplify it.

options: Per-layer SQNR or cosine similarity between float and quantized activations

items.q: What role does ONNX play, and where does it break down?
items.a_short: A vendor-neutral graph format for moving models between frameworks and runtimes. It breaks on custom ops, opset mismatches, and dynamic control flow.
items.a_full: The common failure: a model exports fine but the target runtime doesn't support an op at that opset version, so it silently falls back to CPU. Always run `onnx.checker`, simplify the graph (onnx-simplifier), and verify numerics against the source framework before converting further. Dynamic shapes and Python-level control flow in `forward` are the usual culprits.

options: A neutral graph interchange format; it breaks on custom ops, opset mismatch and dynamic control flow

items.q: What is a TFLite delegate?
items.a_short: A plugin that hands part of the graph to a hardware backend — GPU, NNAPI, Hexagon, Core ML — while the TFLite interpreter runs the rest.
items.a_full: The delegate claims the subgraphs it supports. Too many unsupported ops fragments the graph into many partitions, and each boundary costs a data transfer. Checking the partition count is one of the first things to do when a hardware-accelerated model is slower than expected.

options: A plugin that offloads supported subgraphs to a hardware backend

items.q: A model hits its latency target in the lab but misses it on a phone after 30 seconds. Why?
items.a_short: Thermal throttling. Sustained inference heats the SoC and the governor drops clocks, so steady-state performance is well below peak.
items.a_full: Always benchmark sustained performance, not a burst — run for minutes and report the steady-state percentile, not the best run. Other suspects: the big/little core the thread landed on, DVFS ramp-up latency on the first inferences, and other apps competing for memory bandwidth.

options: Thermal throttling reduces sustained clocks below peak

items.q: Why is a KV cache essential for on-device LLM inference, and what does it cost?
items.a_short: Without it, generating each token re-computes attention over the whole prefix — O(n²) total. With it, each step is O(n). The cost is memory that grows linearly with context.
items.a_full: KV cache size = 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × bytes. For a 7B model at 4k context in FP16 that's gigabytes — often exceeding the weights themselves on a phone. Mitigations: grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads), sliding-window attention, and quantizing the cache to INT8 or INT4.

options: It avoids recomputing attention over the prefix each token, at the cost of memory linear in context

items.q: FP32, FP16, BF16, INT8, INT4 — what distinguishes them?
items.a_short: BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent with fewer mantissa bits, so it has FP32's range but less precision. FP16 has more precision but a narrow range that overflows easily. INT8/INT4 are fixed-point with an explicit scale.
items.a_full: BF16 is the training default on modern accelerators precisely because its range avoids the loss-scaling gymnastics FP16 needs. For inference at the edge, INT8 is the workhorse and INT4 is used for weight-only quantization of LLMs, where memory bandwidth dominates.

options: BF16 has more precision than FP16
BF16 trades mantissa bits for FP32's exponent range; FP16 has more precision but narrow range

items.q: Why are MobileNet, EfficientNet and friends designed differently from ResNet?
items.a_short: They optimize for FLOPs, parameters and memory access on constrained hardware rather than raw accuracy — depthwise separable convs, inverted residuals, and compound scaling.
items.a_full: MobileNetV2's inverted residual expands channels, does a cheap depthwise conv, then projects back down, with the skip connection on the narrow ends to minimize memory. EfficientNet scales depth, width and resolution together via a compound coefficient. Hardware-aware NAS goes further by using measured on-device latency, not FLOPs, as the search objective — because the two correlate poorly.

options: They optimize for FLOPs/memory on constrained hardware via depthwise separable convs and inverted residuals
They are trained differently but architecturally identical

items.q: What's your checklist before shipping a model to a device?
items.a_short: Verify numerics against the float baseline, fold BN, quantize and measure per-layer SQNR, benchmark sustained on-device latency, check operator coverage, and measure memory peak and energy.
items.a_full: Also: confirm preprocessing matches exactly between training and device (resize interpolation and normalization constants are a classic mismatch), test the cold-start path including model load time, and keep the float model available for A/B comparison on real inputs.

options: Just check accuracy on the test set
Numerics vs float, BN folding, per-layer SQNR, sustained latency, op coverage, memory and energy

items.q: If weights and activations are INT8, why is the accumulator INT32?
items.a_short: Products of two INT8 values need 16 bits, and summing thousands of them in a convolution would overflow anything smaller.
items.a_full: A 3×3×256 convolution accumulates 2304 products. INT32 gives headroom with no risk of wraparound. The accumulator is then requantized back to INT8 by multiplying by the combined scale (implemented as a fixed-point multiply plus a right shift, since the hardware avoids floating point) and adding the output zero-point.

options: INT8×INT8 needs 16 bits and summing thousands of products would overflow a smaller accumulator

items.q: What is Q-format fixed-point notation?
items.a_short: Qm.n means m integer bits and n fractional bits in an integer word — the value is `raw / 2ⁿ`.
items.a_full: Q1.15 in a 16-bit word represents [−1, 1) with a step of 2⁻¹⁵. Multiplying two Qm.n numbers gives Q2m.2n, so you must shift right by n to restore the format — forgetting that shift is the classic fixed-point DSP bug. Quantization scales that are powers of two reduce to pure shifts, which is why some runtimes constrain scales that way.

options: m fractional bits, n integer bits
m integer bits and n fractional bits; value = raw / 2^n
